# Ingestion

*LLM first draft · unedited*

## The right answer, buried in forty pages

The help desk from the Embeddings Module keeps one file: a handbook
covering everything the company supports. Section one is car trouble.
Section two is the canteen's banana bread. Section three is how to reset
a password.

Someone types **my car will not start**. This search compares meaning
rather than spelling, so it does find the handbook. What it hands back
is the handbook — forty pages of it, with the two sentences that answer
the question somewhere in the middle.

Nothing is broken. The handbook went into the search as one piece, so
one piece is the smallest thing the search can return. This Module is
about the work that has to happen **before** anyone asks anything, so
that a search has something answer-sized to hand back.

## Ingestion is four moves: load, split, embed, store

**Ingestion** is the work of turning files you already have into a pile
of small searchable pieces. It is four moves in a row, and the rest of
this page takes one section each.

1. **Load** — read the file and turn it into text, plus a note of where
   the text came from.
2. **Split** — cut that text into small pieces.
3. **Embed** — turn each piece into a list of numbers.
4. **Store** — keep those numbers somewhere they can be searched.

None of it happens while a reader waits. Ingestion runs ahead of time,
once per file, and the last section on this page says what that buys.

## Load: a file becomes a document with a label

A **loader** is library code that knows how to read one kind of source —
a PDF, a web page, a folder of text files — and hands back the same
shape whatever it read. That shape is a **document**: the text itself,
plus **metadata**, which is a short set of labels saying where the text
came from. `source: handbook.pdf` and `page: 12` are metadata.

Loaders look like the dull stage, and they decide something that cannot
be recovered later. The labels a loader attaches are the only way a
search hit will ever be able to say which file and which page it came
from. Throw them away here and no later stage can put them back.

## Why the whole handbook does not work

Storing a forty-page file as one piece goes wrong twice over.

The first problem is size. Whatever reads the result afterwards — a
person, or a chat model with a **context limit**, meaning a cap on how
much text it can take in at once — has to wade through the whole file
to reach two sentences.

The second problem is subtler, and it is worth working by hand. Pretend
each text becomes two numbers: the first is how much it is about
vehicles, the second how much it is about food. Real ones run to
hundreds of numbers with no such tidy meaning, and two is enough here.

- the car section → `[2, 1]`
- the banana bread section → `[0, 4]`
- the question "my car will not start" → `[3, 1]`

Embed the handbook as one text and what comes back points between its
sections — near `[2, 5]`, the two section arrows added together.

**Cosine similarity** is the number that says whether two of these
arrows point the same way: 1 is the same direction, 0 is unrelated. It
is the dot product — matching numbers multiplied and added — divided by
the two arrow lengths multiplied together. The Embeddings Module works
through why; the arithmetic is short enough to check here.

- the question against the whole handbook: `(3 × 2) + (1 × 5) = 11`,
  lengths `√10 ≈ 3.16` and `√29 ≈ 5.39`, so
  `11 ÷ (3.16 × 5.39) ≈ 0.65`
- the question against the car section alone: `(3 × 2) + (1 × 1) = 7`,
  lengths `3.16` and `√5 ≈ 2.24`, so `7 ÷ (3.16 × 2.24) ≈ 0.99`

0.65 against 0.99. The car section never moved. Binding banana bread to
it dragged the arrow up and away from the question, and that is the
whole problem in one number: **a document's vector is a blur of every
topic inside it**. The more a file covers, the blurrier it gets, and the
less any one question points at it.

## Split: chunk size and overlap

A **chunk** is one of the small pieces a text gets cut into, and
**chunking** is the cutting. Two settings decide how it goes.

**Chunk size** is how much text goes in one chunk, counted in
characters. Both directions cost something.

- Small chunks have sharp meaning, because there is only one topic in
  each. A chunk too small stops holding a whole answer.
- Big chunks keep more context around each sentence, and drift back
  towards the blur above.

Around 1000 characters is a common starting point, and it is a starting
point rather than a rule — the right size depends on how the source is
written.

**Overlap** is how much of the end of one chunk gets repeated at the
start of the next. It exists because cuts land mid-thought. The two
sentences that answer our question read:

"In cold weather the engine may fail to turn over. Hold the key down for
ten seconds before releasing it."

Cut between them with no overlap and one chunk states a problem with no
fix, while the next states a fix that never mentions cold weather or an
engine. Neither chunk answers the question on its own, and the answer
was in the file the whole time. Repeat the tail of each chunk at the
head of the next and the thought survives the cut, whole, in one chunk.

Overlap is paid for in chunks. Chunk size minus overlap is the **step**
— how far along the text each new chunk starts.

- size `100`, overlap `20`, so step `100 − 20 = 80`
- a 300-character section gives chunks starting at `0`, `80`, `160` and
  `240` — four chunks
- with no overlap the step is `100`, the starts are `0`, `100`, `200`,
  and the same section gives three

More overlap means more chunks, more vectors, more storage, and the same
sentence coming back in two different hits. Overlap of a fifth of the
chunk size or less is the usual compromise.

One more thing helps here: a splitter that cuts at natural boundaries.
`RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` tries paragraph breaks first, then line
breaks, then sentence ends, and only falls back to cutting mid-word when
a stretch of text offers it nothing better.

## Embed: one vector per chunk

Each chunk now goes through an **embedding model** — a program that
takes text in and gives back a fixed-length list of numbers, called a
**vector**, arranged so that texts with similar meaning come back with
similar numbers. That one sentence is all this page needs; the
Embeddings Module is there when you want the rest.

Two habits carry over from it. Chunks and questions have to be embedded
by the same model, because numbers from two different models are not
comparable. And the same text always comes back with the same vector,
which is why the vectors are worth working out once and keeping.

Libraries take the whole pile at once rather than one chunk at a time —
`embed_documents(texts)` in LangChain — which is one network call
instead of a hundred.

## Store: a vector store holds three things per chunk

A **vector store** is a database built for one question: given this
vector, which stored vectors point most nearly the same way? It answers
that using an **index**, an arrangement of the data that makes lookup
fast without comparing the asked-for vector against every row.

Each row holds three things, and each earns its place.

- **The vector** — what actually gets compared. Nothing else in the row
  is searched.
- **The chunk's text** — what gets handed back. A vector cannot be
  turned back into its text, so if the row does not keep the text, the
  text is gone.
- **The metadata** — `source`, `page`, whatever the loader attached. A
  hit that cannot name its file cannot be checked by the person reading
  it.

Chroma, FAISS and pgvector are three of the common ones. Which you pick
is a line of setup; the four moves on this page do not change.

## Ingestion runs before question time

Everything above happens once per document, ahead of any question. When
a question does arrive, the work is short: embed the question with the
same model, ask the store for the nearest rows, and read what comes
back. That is why the slow stages sit here rather than in the reader's
wait.

Two forward references, each its own Module and neither needed to
finish this one.

- **Retrieval-Augmented Generation** — hand those nearest chunks to a
  chat model so its answer is built out of your documents.
- **Agents & Tool Use** — a model that decides for itself when to go
  searching.

The one maintenance job ingestion creates: when a file changes, its
chunks have to be re-ingested. The store keeps answering with the old
text until they are, and it has no way of knowing the file moved on.

## The short version

- Ingestion is load, split, embed, store — all of it before anyone asks
  a question, and again whenever a document changes.
- A loader turns a file into a document: text plus metadata saying where
  the text came from. Labels dropped here cannot be recovered later.
- A whole document embedded whole is a blur of every topic in it: 0.65
  against the question, where its car section alone came out at 0.99.
- Chunk size sets how sharp each piece is; overlap repeats the tail of
  one chunk at the head of the next so a thought cut in half survives.
- A vector store row is a vector to search, the text to hand back, and
  metadata to prove where the text came from.

modelExamples.before:
# The handbook goes into the store whole: one file, one row, one vector.
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings

handbook = open("handbook.txt").read()
print(len(handbook))
# 96412

store = Chroma(
    embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small"),
)
store.add_texts([handbook])

hit = store.similarity_search("my car will not start", k=1)[0]
print(len(hit.page_content))
# 96412

# The only row in the store is the whole handbook, so the whole
# handbook is the smallest thing a search can hand back — forty pages
# around the two sentences that answer the question. Its one vector is
# a blur of car trouble, banana bread and password resets, so no
# question points at it strongly either.
modelExamples.after:
# The same handbook, cut up first. Two settings decide the cutting, and
# the splitter prefers paragraph breaks to cutting mid-word.
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

handbook = open("handbook.txt").read()

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=1000,
    chunk_overlap=200,
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(handbook)
print(len(chunks))
# 121

store = Chroma(
    embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small"),
)
store.add_texts(chunks)

hit = store.similarity_search("my car will not start", k=1)[0]
print(hit.page_content)
# In cold weather the engine may fail to turn over. Hold the key down
# for ten seconds before releasing it. ...

# 121 rows where there was 1. Each row covers one topic, so its vector
# points at that topic instead of at the average of forty pages, and
# what comes back is an answer rather than a document to search by eye.
modelExamples.caption: What moved: the size of the thing being compared. Before, one file is one row, so the whole handbook is both what gets embedded and what comes back — its vector averages car trouble, banana bread and password resets, and the reader still has forty pages to search by eye. After, the same text is cut into chunks with a size and an overlap first, so each row covers one topic and the search hands back the two sentences that answer the question. The handbook did not change and the search did not change; what got stored did.

modelExamples.before:
# Three files, chunked and stored as bare strings: the text goes in,
# where it came from does not.
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200)

chunks = []
for name in ["handbook.pdf", "canteen.pdf", "it-policy.pdf"]:
    for page in PyPDFLoader(name).load():
        chunks.extend(splitter.split_text(page.page_content))

store = Chroma(
    embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small"),
)
store.add_texts(chunks)

hit = store.similarity_search("my car will not start", k=1)[0]
print(hit.page_content)
# In cold weather the engine may fail to turn over. ...
print(hit.metadata)
# {}

# The passage is the right one and nobody can check it. Reading
# page.page_content took the text and left the loader's labels behind,
# so the row cannot name its file or its page, and no later stage can
# work out what that loop threw away.
modelExamples.after:
# The same three files kept as documents — text plus the labels saying
# where the text came from — all the way into the store.
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

documents = []
for name in ["handbook.pdf", "canteen.pdf", "it-policy.pdf"]:
    # One document per page, each carrying source and page already.
    documents.extend(PyPDFLoader(name).load())

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(documents)

store = Chroma(
    embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small"),
)
store.add_documents(chunks)

hit = store.similarity_search("my car will not start", k=1)[0]
print(hit.page_content)
# In cold weather the engine may fail to turn over. ...
print(hit.metadata)
# {'source': 'handbook.pdf', 'page': 12}

# split_documents copies each document's metadata onto every chunk cut
# from it, so the labels ride all the way through. An answer citing
# handbook.pdf page 12 can be opened and checked; an answer citing
# nothing has to be taken on trust.
modelExamples.caption: What got kept: where the text came from. Before, the loader's labels are read off and dropped the moment the page's text is passed to the splitter, so a hit arrives with empty metadata and no later stage can work out which of the three files it was cut from. After, the documents stay documents through the split, and split_documents copies each one's source and page onto every chunk cut from it. The passage returned is the same either way — the difference is that one of them can be opened and checked.

Chunking is what gives each topic a vector of its own to be found by.
